blocks.text: Pediatric eye examination is a common OSCE station because it tests both technique and your ability to recognize conditions that can threaten vision.
GENERAL → VISUAL ACUITY → INSPECTION → PUPILS → EYE MOVEMENTS → ALIGNMENT → ANTERIOR SEGMENT → RED REFLEX → FUNDOSCOPY → VISION-SPECIFIC TESTS
For a complete pediatric eye examination, remember:
A — Appearance V — Visual acuity P — Pupils M — Movements A — Alignment R — Red reflex F — Fundoscopy

“This is a well-appearing child with no abnormal head posture or obvious ocular asymmetry. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally. The eyelids and conjunctivae are normal, with clear corneas and no discharge. The pupils are equal, round and reactive to light, with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Extraocular movements are full and conjugate, with no nystagmus. The eyes are aligned normally on corneal light reflex and cover testing. Red reflexes are symmetrical bilaterally, and fundoscopy shows normal optic discs and retinal appearances. Overall, this is a normal ocular examination.”
This is particularly important for your exam.

“There is bilateral conjunctival injection with mucopurulent discharge and crusting of the eyelids. Visual acuity is preserved, the pupils are normal, and there is no corneal opacity or significant photophobia. The findings are most consistent with acute conjunctivitis.”

“The left optic disc is diffusely pale compared with the right, with otherwise preserved disc margins. This is consistent with left optic atrophy in the appropriate clinical context.”

“There is unilateral right-sided proptosis with periorbital swelling and restricted ocular movement. The child also has reduced visual acuity on the affected side. These are concerning orbital findings requiring urgent ophthalmological assessment.”

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What is the most important cause of leukocoria to exclude?

blocks.text: It is a potentially life-threatening malignant eye tumor in children, and early diagnosis can be vision- and life-saving.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What are the causes of leukocoria?

blocks.text: Retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, Coats disease, retinal detachment, persistent fetal vasculature and retinopathy of prematurity.
Reduced visual acuity resulting from abnormal visual development during childhood, without an adequate structural explanation for the degree of visual loss.
Significant asymmetry in the afferent visual pathway, commonly from optic nerve or severe retinal disease.

Q9. What is the difference between esotropia and exotropia?

blocks.text: Esotropia is inward deviation of the eye; exotropia is outward deviation.

content_groups.group_title: Q10. Why is early detection of strabismus important?

blocks.text: Because persistent misalignment during visual development can cause amblyopia and impaired binocular vision.
Raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise.

content_groups.group_title: Q12. What is the significance of a painful red eye?

blocks.text: It raises concern for more serious ocular pathology such as keratitis, corneal ulcer or uveitis, particularly when associated with photophobia or reduced vision.
